rules.claim: A seed comes up from the warmth of the soil, not from a date on the calendar. Each kind of seed has a soil-temperature range it germinates in; sown into ground colder than that range it comes up slowly and patchily or rots before it can emerge, and ground hotter than the range stalls it too.
rules.mechanism: Germination is driven by temperature-dependent enzymes that mobilise the seed's stored reserves, so in soil below the species' range those enzymes work too slowly for the seedling to emerge before soil fungi rot the water-swollen seed, and in soil above the range that same enzyme machinery is suppressed. That is why the soil's own temperature is the reliable signal, and the day of the year is not.
sources: OSU Extension Service / J. F. Harrington (Dept. of Vegetable Crops, Univ. of California, Davis), 'Soil temperature conditions for vegetable seed germination', extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/soil-temperature-conditions-vegetable-seed-germination (published April 2013, reviewed 2024; fetched in-container 2026-09-20, read by the maintainer 2026-09-20): the table 'Days to appearance of seedlings at various soil temperatures' gives an optimum soil temperature per crop (e.g. bean optimum 80 F, lettuce 75 F, asparagus 75 F) and marks 'Little or no germination' at the cold end of each crop's row (e.g. bean at temperatures below 50 F). It states the germination range but does not state the cold-soil rot mechanism, which the Wisconsin source below supplies.

UW-Madison Extension, Wisconsin Horticulture / Lisa Johnson, 'When Is the Right Time to Plant Vegetable Seeds? Check Soil Temperature', hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/when-is-the-right-time-to-plant-vegetable-seeds-check-soil-temperature (revised January 2025; fetched in-container 2026-09-20, read 2026-09-20): 'In our rapidly changing climate, a calendar date is not the best predictor for an extra early onset of spring weather in March or an extremely late, cold and wet April'; 'A better method to gauge when to put seeds in the ground is to test soil temperatures'; 'If you plant too early in cold soil, the seed may rot, but if it does germinate, it will be slow to do so and likely to produce stunted plants that are more prone to disease.'

rules.claim: Some seed will not germinate straight from the packet. It carries a built-in dormancy that a pre-sow treatment has to break first. A hard-coated seed is scarified or soaked so water can get in; a seed with internal dormancy is cold-moist stratified (chilled damp for weeks) before it will come up. The treatment has to be started far enough ahead of the sowing date to finish in time.
rules.mechanism: A hard, water-impermeable seed coat holds the seed dormant by blocking imbibition, so nicking, abrading, or soaking the coat is what lets water reach the embryo; a seed with physiological dormancy stays shut until a period of cold, moist chilling lets its germination-inhibiting hormones dissipate. So each treatment takes its own span of time, and starting it late leaves the seed still dormant at sowing.
sources: Penn State Extension / Tianna DuPont, 'Seed and Seedling Biology', extension.psu.edu/seed-and-seedling-biology (updated January 14, 2025; fetched in-container 2026-09-20, read by the maintainer 2026-09-20): 'Seeds might have a hard or thick seed coat (physical dormancy). This can be broken by soaking or scarifying (scratching the surface) the seed'; and on imbibition, 'The seed rapidly takes up water and the seed coat swells and softens.'

UW-Madison Extension, Wisconsin Horticulture / Bruce Spangenberg, 'Plant Dormancy a Dependable Process', hort.extension.wisc.edu/plant-dormancy-a-dependable-process (fetched in-container 2026-09-20, read 2026-09-20): 'A tough seed coat prevents water uptake and seed germination'; 'Seeds collected from native plants are often recommended to be mixed with abrasive sand or even roughened with a file; this breaks physical dormancy'; and on cold stratification, 'After exposure to a certain length of winter cold, abscisic acid levels dissipate in seeds', with 'Typically, minimum temperatures range from upper thirties to 40 degrees Fahrenheit.'

rules.claim: A few kinds of seed need light to germinate, and burying them stops them coming up. Sow these on the surface, pressed into firm, moist soil and left uncovered or barely dusted over. Don't sow them at the depth a larger seed would take.
rules.mechanism: These seeds carry the light-sensing pigment phytochrome, which must catch light to switch on the hormone cascade that releases the seed to germinate, so a seed buried past a few millimeters sits in the dark with that switch never thrown and stays dormant.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Handbook, ch. 13 'Propagation' / Anthony V. LeBude & Frank A. Blazich (NC State Extension, 2022), content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/13-propagation (fetched in-container 2026-09-20, read by the maintainer 2026-09-20): 'When sowing light-requiring seeds, sow them on the soil surface'; the plants it lists as requiring light for germination are 'ageratum, begonia, browallia, impatiens, lettuce, and petunia'; and 'Extremely fine seeds such as carrot, petunia, and snapdragon should not be covered, but simply dusted on the surface of the germinating medium and watered with a fine mist.' The page states the practice, not the phytochrome mechanism.

rules.claim: White powdery spots on squash, cucumber, melon or pumpkin leaves are powdery mildew, a fungus that spreads on the wind and strikes the older leaves first. It weakens the plant and the fruit ripens early.
rules.mechanism: The fungus (mainly Podosphaera xanthii) grows on the leaf surface; the spores formed in each spot are carried by the wind to other leaves, and under favorable conditions it spreads until it covers most of the foliage. A plant that loses most of its leaf area to it is weakened, and its fruit ripens prematurely. It takes hold most readily on densely planted vines, plants crowded by weeds, plants in shade and over-fertilized plants.
sources: UMN Extension, 'Powdery mildew of cucurbits', extension.umn.edu/agriculture/specialty-crops/vegetable-farming/disease-management/powdery-mildew-of-cucurbits (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'White powdery spots can form on both upper and lower leaf surfaces, and quickly expand into large blotches.'; 'When powdery mildew infects the majority of the foliage, the plant becomes weak and the fruit ripens prematurely.'; 'The older leaves are more susceptible and powdery mildew will infect them first.'; 'Wind blows spores produced in leaf spots to infect other leaves.'; 'Powdery mildew is more likely to infect densely planted vines, plants crowded by weeds, plants in shaded sites and over-fertilized plants.'; 'Plant varieties with complete or partial resistance to powdery mildew.'; 'Provide good air movement around plants through proper spacing, staking of plants, and weed control.'; 'Powdery mildew, mainly caused by the fungus Podosphaera xanthii , infects all cucurbits, including muskmelons, squash, cucumbers, gourds, watermelons and pumpkins.'; 'If susceptible varieties are growing in an area where powdery mildew has resulted in yield loss in the past, fungicide applications may be necessary.'; 'Monitor for the presence of powdery mildew, and start fungicide treatments when disease is first found.'

rules.claim: Small, soft, pear-shaped insects clustered on a plant, with twisted and curled leaves, are aphids. They feed on the sap; heavy feeding yellows and stunts the plant.
rules.mechanism: Aphids feed on plant sap, injecting saliva into the host as they feed. Severe feeding twists and curls the leaves, yellows the foliage, stunts or kills shoots and slows growth. They secrete a sticky, sugary honeydew that can let sooty mold grow on the leaves, though the honeydew itself does not harm the plant.
sources: UMN Extension, 'Aphids in home yards and gardens', extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/yard-and-garden-insects/aphids (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'Aphids are small, 1/16- to 1/8-inch-long (2-4 mm), pear-shaped, soft-bodied insects.'; 'Signs of severe aphid feeding are twisted and curled leaves, yellowed leaves, stunted or dead shoots and poor plant growth.'; 'When aphids feed, they inject saliva into their host plant to help digest the sap.'; 'Honeydew generally does not cause any harm, but can cause leaves to stick together and can encourage the growth of sooty mold.'; 'You can physically knock aphids off plants with a strong spray of water from a garden hose.'; 'Protect natural enemies by avoiding pesticide applications or using low risk products.'; 'Insecticidal soap, horticultural oil and pyrethrins can be effective at controlling aphids.'; 'There are many natural enemies of aphids that are commonly found in gardens, including lady beetles , lacewings , syrphid fly larvae and parasitic wasps.'; 'Encourage natural enemies by planting flowering plants that blossom at different times of the growing season.'

rules.claim: Brown leaf spots with target-like rings, starting on the lower leaves of tomato or potato, are early blight, a fungus that overwinters in plant debris and soil and reaches the leaves by soil splash.
rules.mechanism: The early blight fungi overwinter in infected plant debris and in the soil. Lower leaves are infected when they touch contaminated soil or when rain splashes soil up onto them; the spores need free water or very high humidity to germinate. Spots enlarge with concentric rings, and fruit can form leathery black spots.
sources: UMN Extension, 'Early blight in tomato and potato', extension.umn.edu/agriculture/specialty-crops/vegetable-farming/disease-management/early-blight-in-tomato-and-potato (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'Larger spots have target-like concentric rings.'; 'The early blight pathogens both overwinter in infected plant debris and soil in Minnesota.'; 'Lower leaves become infected when they come into contact with contaminated soil, either through direct contact or when raindrops splash soil onto the leaves.'; 'Cover the soil under the plants with mulch, such as fabric, straw, plastic mulch, or dried leaves.'; 'Water at the base of each plant, using drip irrigation, a soaker hose, or careful hand watering.'; 'Do not remove more than one-third of the plant's leaves.'; 'Rotate out of tomatoes and related crops for at least two years.'; 'Spores (reproductive structures) can germinate between 47° and 90° F and need free water or relative humidity of 90% or greater.'; 'Fruit spots are leathery and black, with raised concentric ridges.'; 'Staking will also reduce contact between the leaves and spore-contaminated soil.'; 'Remove leaves with leaf spots and bury or burn them.'; 'There are many resistant tomato cultivars available, often designated with an "EB" in seed catalogs.'; 'In the fall, remove or bury infected plants to reduce the likelihood of the pathogen surviving into the following year.'

rules.claim: A squash or pumpkin runner that suddenly wilts, with sawdust-like frass pushed out of holes in the stem near the wilt, has a squash vine borer inside. The larva feeds in the vine and cuts off its water.
rules.mechanism: The adult is a day-flying moth that lays its eggs singly at the base of the plant, on leaf stalks and on vines. The larvae tunnel into the stem to feed, and their feeding destroys the vine's vascular tissue, stopping water and nutrient movement, and that is the sudden wilt. As they feed they push frass out of holes in the side of the stem.
sources: UW-Madison Extension (Wisconsin Horticulture), 'Squash Vine Borer, Melittia cucurbitae', hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/squash-vine-borer-melittia-curcurbitae/ (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'If you've ever had a squash or pumpkin plant with one or more runners that suddenly wilt and then die, it was mostly likely infested by squash vine borer.'; 'Their feeding within the vines destroys the vascular tissues of the plant, preventing water movement and nutrient transfer, which leads to the characteristic wilting.'; 'As they feed, they push their sawdust-like fecal matter (frass) out of holes in the side of the stem near the wilting point.'; 'At the first sight of frass, homeowners can carefully slit the vine lengthwise near the damaged area and remove the larvae.'; 'Plants can be covered with floating row cover but only where squash didn't grow the previous year.'; 'The adult squash vine borer is a day-flying moth, with a distinctive superficial appearance more like a wasp than a moth.'; 'Females lay up to 250 small flattened, oval, and dull-red to brown eggs individually, rather than in groups, on the base of plants, leaf stalks, and vines which are almost impossible to spot.'; 'For vining (not bush) varieties, try burying a few nodes along each vine so the plant will root at these nodes and less the impact of the pest if it does infest the base of the vine.'

rules.claim: Lower tomato leaves that yellow after dark spots appear have a fungal leaf disease (early blight or Septoria leaf spot); leaves that yellow without spots, especially in containers, can be short of nitrogen.
rules.mechanism: Early blight and Septoria leaf spot are fungal diseases that begin on the lower foliage in wet weather as deep brown or blackish spots, followed by yellowing or browning of the leaves. Early blight has target-like rings, and Septoria has whitish centers and dark borders. Separately, tomato leaves can yellow from a lack of nitrogen, which is common in containers because frequent watering and low soil fertility leave little of it.
sources: UW-Madison Extension (Wisconsin Horticulture), 'Troubleshooting Tomato Problems', hort.extension.wisc.edu/troubleshooting-tomato-problems/ (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'Early blight and septoria leafspot are fungal leaf diseases infecting tomato plants, especially during wet weather.'; 'Initial symptoms typically appear on the lower foliage of plants, starting as deep brown or blackish spots, followed by yellowing or browning of leaves.'; 'Early blight spots will develop concentric rings and a target-like appearance, often with a yellow halo. Septoria spots typically have whitish centers and dark borders.'; 'Tomato leaves may also show yellowing from lack of nitrogen. This is especially common in containers, due to frequent watering and low soil fertility.'; 'Adding nitrogen fertilizer will help alleviate this problem but be careful not to over-apply.'; 'Removing infected leaves, or even entire plants, might help reduce spreading of disease.'; 'Mulching will help reduce soil splashing onto lower foliage, which often includes fungal spores.'; 'Improve air circulation around tomato plants by avoiding closely spaced plantings, using cages, or staking.'; 'In future years, practice crop rotation and choose early blight- and septoria-resistant tomato cultivars.'

rules.claim: Large, ragged holes chewed in cabbage, broccoli or kale leaves, with velvety green caterpillars on them, are imported cabbageworm, the larva of the white butterflies that lay on cole crops.
rules.mechanism: The adult is a white butterfly with black spots on its forewings that lays its eggs on cole crops. The caterpillars grow to about an inch, velvety green with faint yellow stripes, and the larger ones chew large, ragged holes in the leaves, leaving the big veins.
sources: UMN Extension, 'Caterpillars on cole crops', extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/yard-and-garden-insects/caterpillars-on-cole-crops (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'Adults are white butterflies with black spots on the forewings.'; 'Caterpillars can grow up to 1 inch in length and are velvety green with faint yellow stripes running lengthwise down the back and sides.'; 'Larger caterpillars chew large, ragged holes in the leaves leaving the large veins intact.'; 'Handpick and drop the caterpillars into a pail of soapy water to kill them.'; 'Floating row covers made up of lightweight all-purpose garden fabric keep the adult moths from laying eggs on plants.'; 'Fit the row covers directly over garden plants or over metal hoops/wooden frame to cover the cole crops at seeding or transplanting.'; 'When diamondback moths are the dominant caterpillar found, or when other caterpillars are found while they are still young, consider using a Bt product.'

rules.claim: A winter cover crop is sown in autumn a set time before the first fall frost (about six to eight weeks for crimson clover, 30 to 45 days for hairy vetch, four to six weeks for cereal rye), so it roots and grows before winter.
rules.mechanism: The plants need time to germinate and grow before the first hard frost and short days force them into dormancy; sown too late, a cover crop neither covers the soil through winter nor survives to grow again in spring. Sown too early, crimson clover can go to seed in the fall and not regrow until the soil warms. Cereal rye tolerates the latest sowing of the three.
sources: University of Maryland Extension, 'Cover Crops For Gardens', extension.umd.edu/resource/cover-crops-gardens (fetched in-container 2026-09-25, read by the maintainer 2026-09-25): 'Fall-sown cover crops are typically planted in a two-month window, starting in mid-August and ending no later than mid-October. rules.claim: Very tender crops go out about two weeks after the average last spring frost: tomato, pepper, eggplant, lima beans, melons, watermelon, pumpkin and winter squash. Tender crops go in at the frost itself (R-031).
rules.mechanism: Chilling. A very tender crop is hurt by cool weather as well as by frost: it needs daytime temperatures above 60 F, and a week of days below 55 F can stunt it. Setting it out about two weeks after the average last frost gives the days time to warm.
sources: Colorado State Univ. Extension, GardenNotes #720, 'Vegetable Planting Guide', extension.colostate.edu/resource/vegetable-planting-guide (fetched in-container 2026-09-30; read by the maintainer 2026-09-30): 'Very Tender Vegetables', 'Crops: lima beans, cantaloupe, eggplant, pepper, pumpkin, winter squash and pumpkins, tomato, and watermelon'; 'Very tender vegetables are not only intolerant of frost, but also cool spring winds. A week of daytime temperatures below 55F may stunt the crop.'; when to plant, 'Typically 2+ weeks after the average last spring frost date'.

rules.claim: A lettuce or spinach sowing that comes ready in a month whose normal daytime high reaches the crop's bolting temperature (about 24 C, 75 F), while days are longer than nights, is likely to bolt before it can be picked.
rules.mechanism: Long days and several days in a row above about 24 C (75 F) switch lettuce and spinach from making leaves to making a flower stalk, which turns the leaves bitter and ends the harvest.
sources: UMN Extension, 'Growing lettuce, endive and radicchio in home gardens' (reviewed in 2024), extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/growing-lettuce-endive-and-radicchio (fetched in-container 2026-10-10; read by the maintainer 2026-10-09, D-281): 'Multiple days of high temperatures (greater than 75° F) can cause lettuce plants to flower.'; 'For most places in Minnesota, June, July and August conditions are too hot for these crops. These plants may bolt in response to long days, high light intensity, and heat.'; 'Bolting ends the possibility of harvest.'; 'For a fall crop, sow seed about three months before the average first fall frost date.'

UMN Extension, 'Growing spinach and Swiss chard in home gardens' (reviewed in 2022), extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/growing-spinach-and-swiss-chard (fetched in-container 2026-10-10; read by the maintainer 2026-10-09, D-281): 'Spinach plants can start to flower after multiple days of high temperatures (greater than 75° F).'; 'Spinach plants respond to increasing day length by "bolting:" sending up a flowering stalk'; 'During May, the days are much longer than the nights.'; 'Spinach planted in August for a fall crop will grow under shortening days, and will not bolt.'; 'For a fall crop, sow seed two months before the average first frost date.'

rules.claim: A bed under a roof, a patio cover or indoors gets no rain, so all of its water comes from you, whatever the weather.
rules.mechanism: The roof or ceiling stops the rain before it reaches the soil, so a wet week outside adds nothing to the water in the bed.
sources: definition

rules.claim: A growing vegetable garden needs about an inch of water a week (25 mm), rain and watering counted together. In a month whose normal rain falls short of that, an open bed's watering makes up the difference, and where the rain falls below a quarter of it, nearly every drop is yours.
rules.mechanism: Growing plants draw water out of the soil, and sun and air dry it from the top. What the rain does not put back, the soil loses until it is watered.
sources: UMN Extension, Natalie Hoidal, 'Gardening in hot weather' (reviewed in 2025), extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/gardening-hot-weather (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'The average vegetable garden needs about 1 inch of rain per week. This looks like: 62 gallons for a 10x10-foot area. About 20 gallons for a 4x8-foot raised bed.'

UA Cooperative Extension, Yavapai County Master Gardeners, 'Backyard Vegetable Garden Irrigation' (no date), extension.arizona.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/BackyardIrrigationBillMains.pdf (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'While growing, vegetable crops need about an inch of water per week in the form of rainwater, irrigation water, or both'

UMN Extension, 'Growing lettuce, endive and radicchio in home gardens' (reviewed in 2024), extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/growing-lettuce-endive-and-radicchio (fetched in-container 2026-10-10; read by the maintainer 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-11): 'One inch of rainfall per week is adequate.'

NC State Extension, Wilkes County, Matthew Clay, 'Watering Wisely: How Much Your Summer Vegetable Garden Really Needs' (2025-06-30), wilkes.ces.ncsu.edu/news/watering-wisely-how-much-your-summer-vegetable-garden-really-needs/ (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11), the source that words it the other way: 'Most vegetable gardens require approximately one inch of water per week, excluding rainfall.'; 'Just remember to pause watering during rainy weeks, so you're not doubling up.'

rules.claim: In a month whose normal days run above 90 F (32 C) and whose normal nights stay above 70 F (21 C), a vegetable garden may need water daily or every other day.
rules.mechanism: Heat speeds both the water plants draw from the soil and the water the soil loses to the air, so after each watering the soil is dry again sooner.
sources: UMN Extension, Natalie Hoidal, 'Gardening in hot weather' (reviewed in 2025), extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/gardening-hot-weather (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'During extremely hot weather (daytime temperatures above 90°F and nighttime temperatures above 70°F), try to water daily or every other day. In a 10x10-foot garden, this would mean giving your plants 8 to 9 gallons of water each day.'

UA Cooperative Extension, Yavapai County Master Gardeners, 'Backyard Vegetable Garden Irrigation' (no date), extension.arizona.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/BackyardIrrigationBillMains.pdf (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'As a rule, it will be necessary to irrigate your vegetable garden 2 to 4 times a week in the warmest/driest summer months and once or twice per week or less in other seasons.'

rules.claim: In hot weather, water early in the morning, before the heat of the day.
rules.mechanism: Less water evaporates from the soil in the cool of the morning than in the heat of the day, so more of what you give soaks in and reaches the roots.
sources: UMN Extension, Natalie Hoidal, 'Gardening in hot weather' (reviewed in 2025), extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/gardening-hot-weather (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'Water your plants in the morning as early as possible. This allows the soil and your plants to absorb more water because, in the heat of the day, there is more evaporation occurring at the soil surface.'

UA Cooperative Extension, Yavapai County Master Gardeners, 'Backyard Vegetable Garden Irrigation' (no date), extension.arizona.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/BackyardIrrigationBillMains.pdf (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): on furrow and basin watering, 'this technique is subject to a great deal of evaporation in hot dry climates' and 'Watering in the cool of the morning will reduce this'; on sprinklers, 'Watering in the cool of the morning will reduce evaporation as well as allow leaves to dry by day'.

NC State Extension, Wilkes County, Matthew Clay, 'Watering Wisely: How Much Your Summer Vegetable Garden Really Needs' (2025-06-30), wilkes.ces.ncsu.edu/news/watering-wisely-how-much-your-summer-vegetable-garden-really-needs/ (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'Early morning or late evening are generally best, especially during the summer heat wave.'

rules.claim: A layer of organic mulch over the soil cuts the water a bed loses from its surface, and with it the watering the bed needs, by around half in Colorado State's figure.
rules.mechanism: Mulch covers and shades the soil, so less of its water evaporates from the surface and the moisture below stays more even.
sources: CSU Extension GardenNotes #715, Whiting, O'Meara and Wilson, 'Mulches for the Vegetable Garden' (October 2014, reviewed May 2023), extension.colostate.edu/resource/mulches-for-the-vegetable-garden/ (fetched in-container 2026-10-11; read by the maintainer 2026-10-11): 'In general, mulching minimizes evaporation of water from the soil surface, reducing irrigation need by around 50%.'; 'Mulching may cool or warm soil temperatures.'

UMN Extension, 'Mulching for soil and garden health', extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/mulching-for-soil-and-garden-health (read 2026-07-11; confirmed by the maintainer on the 2026-07-13 checklist; also R-053's): 'Studies show that mulch reduces evaporation from the soil surface and helps soil hold water.'

rules.claim: A bean sowing that comes ready in a month whose normal daytime high is 90 F (32 C) or more is likely to drop its flowers and set few pods.
rules.mechanism: Above about 90 F the pollen turns sticky and pollination fails, so the flowers fall without setting pods.
sources: UC Statewide IPM Program, 'Blossom Drop in Beans', ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/GARDEN/VEGES/ENVIRON/blossomdrop.html (no date; fetched in-container 2026-10-14; read by the maintainer 2026-10-14): 'This condition occurs when the temperature is over 90°F, the soil moisture is low, or smog is present during the blossoming period.'; 'Plant early to avoid hot weather during the flowering and fruiting period.'

N.C. rules.claim: Milpa reads every soil pH range and threshold it checks plants against as water pH. A pH a lab measured in calcium chloride, or in another salt solution, is recorded and shown with its method. It is never compared with those numbers, and never converted to water pH by a fixed amount.
rules.mechanism: A pH read in a calcium chloride solution is commonly 0.5 to 1.0 unit lower than the same soil read in water, by an amount that changes with the soil's type and salt content, so a range written in water pH cannot be compared with it or reached by adding a fixed number.

rules.claim: Where frost sets the season, a crop reaches harvest outdoors only where enough months in a row average at least its lowest monthly temperature to cover its days to maturity. Where fewer do, or none, it is a crop to grow with care: under cover, from an early start indoors, or as its quickest variety.
rules.mechanism: A crop grows at the pace its days to maturity assume only in months at least as warm as the low end of its band, and in cooler months it grows too slowly to finish, so a frost-free season of cool months can end before the crop is ready.
sources: UC Cooperative Extension Placer/Nevada Counties, publication 31-043C 'Vegetable Characteristics' (compiled by Cindy Fake, May 2011), oc4h.ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2017-01/142583.pdf (fetched in-container 2026-10-15; read by the maintainer 2026-10-15): 'Optimum Temperatures for Different Vegetables'; 'Optimum Minimum Maximum Vegetable'; '70-85º 65º 95º Eggplant, Ceylon spinach, chili pepper, okra,'; '70-75º 65º 80º Sweet pepper, tomato'; '65-75º 60º 90º Cucumber, cantaloupe'; '65-75º 50º 90º Chayote, pumpkin, squash'; '60-75º 50º 95º Sweet corn, black-eyed pea (cowpea),'; '60-70º 50º 80º Lima bean, snap bean'. The rows give each crop's optimum, minimum and maximum in °F, and each species record quotes its own row; this rule reads the minimum. It is the only source of every floor here.
